title: Space
strapline: Five, four, three, two, one — blast off into the biggest questions a small person can ask.
intent: Harness the countdown, the launch and the mission — space play is number play with a rocket strapped to it.
Build a vocabulary that reaches past the everyday: astronaut, orbit, gravity, crater, launch pad, mission control.
Wonder at real, enormous ideas — day and night, the moon changing shape, how far away the stars are — and honour the questions that follow.
Design and build rockets and rovers with a plan, then redesign when the first launch goes wrong.
Sustain rich mission narratives: moon landings, broken boosters, a crew stranded on Mars awaiting rescue.
implementation: Count down to every launch — backwards from five, then ten — and count the crew aboard before lift-off, every time.
Use mission language in role: 'mission control to rocket one, prepare for landing' — children adopt the register within days.
Build rockets from boxes, tubes and foil with the children's plans leading; when it topples, ask what the engineers should change.
Track the real moon together — send home a moon-spotting card and let children report what shape it was last night.
Darken a den for a 'night sky': torches, star cards and glow stars turn day and night into something children can step into and out of.
Welcome the unanswerable questions and model finding out — 'I don't know why space is dark. Shall we find out together?'
Drop a mission problem into the play — a crater blocks the rover, the oxygen is low — and let the crew solve it.
key_questions: What does your crew need to pack for the moon?
Why do you think the moon looks different tonight than last week?
The booster has broken and you're still in space — what's the plan?
What do you think you'd see out of the rocket window?
How far away is the moon — further than nursery to your house?

impact.text: Children count down from five and ten to launch, and count the astronauts aboard before every lift-off because the mission depends on it.
Children build rockets and rovers with a stated plan — and redesign when the launch topples, talking through what went wrong.
Children use space vocabulary confidently in play — orbit, gravity, crater, astronaut, mission control.
Children talk about the pattern of day following night and the moon changing shape, and predict what comes next.
Children sustain long-running space missions — moon landings, alien rescues, life aboard the station — carrying the story across days.
Children use positional language in flight — orbiting around the planet, landing on the crater's edge, floating between the stars.
Children ask enormous, genuine questions — why is space dark? does anyone live there? — and expect real answers or a real hunt for them.
Children recount their missions in sequence afterwards — the launch, the landing, the trouble and the rescue.

enhancements: A launch-pad countdown board with movable numbers 10 to 1 and a big red 'LAUNCH' button.
A moon-surface tray: flour and gravel for craters, rovers to leave tracks, and flags for planting.
A dark den with torches, glow stars and star-pattern cards for finding shapes in the 'sky'.
Junk-modelling launch bay: boxes, tubes, foil and tape, plus a clipboard for rocket designs before building.
Astronaut role-play kit — helmet, backpack 'oxygen' tanks, mission checklists to tick off.
Frozen 'moon rocks' to excavate with droppers of warm water, then sort and weigh at the lab table.
A moon-diary card sent home: what shape was the moon tonight? Draw it and bring it back.

playing_exploring: Space is the room's biggest 'what if' — children step into an imagined world and make it real with boxes and foil.
The dark den and torch-lit stars let children explore night-time safely inside the day.
active_learning: Rockets fall over; crews rebuild them. The redesign loop is the learning.
A mission has stages — pack, count down, launch, land, return — and children hold the whole sequence to the end.
creating_thinking: Children link the real moon they saw last night to the one in the tray, moving between fact and story.
Mission problems with no script — low oxygen, a blocked crater — demand invented solutions, argued out by the crew.
